name: Pregabalin
sections: White to off-white crystalline solid, freely soluble in water.

Developed as a more potent successor to gabapentin; pain relief may begin within the first week. First approval/introduction: Synthesised 1990 (Richard B. Silverman, Northwestern University); EU and US FDA 2004 (Pfizer).

Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels with higher affinity than gabapentin, decreasing release of excitatory neurotransmitters; analgesic, anxiolytic and anticonvulsant. Receptor / target profile: Binds the alpha-2-delta-1 protein of voltage-gated calcium channels with high affinity, reducing release of glutamate, norepinephrine and substance P.
Summary: Bioavailability ≥90% (linear); Tmax ~1 h. Not protein bound; negligible metabolism. Half-life ~6.3 h. Renally excreted unchanged – adjust dose to CrCl.
Peripheral and central neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, spinal cord injury)
Neuropathic pain: 75 mg twice daily (150 mg/day); increase to 300 mg/day after 3–7 days; max 600 mg/day
Elderly/frail: start 50 mg or 75 mg at bedtime
Renal impairment: CrCl 30–60 – halve dose; 15–30 – quarter dose
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
CrCl ≥60: 150–600 mg/day; 30–60: 75–300; 15–30: 25–150; <15: 25–75 mg/day; supplement after dialysis.
Peripheral oedema – caution in heart failure
With or without food; avoid alcohol.
Renal function; weight; oedema; misuse; respiratory status.
Somnolence, confusion, agitation, restlessness, seizures (rare), coma. Supportive care; haemodialysis effective.
Cochrane review (Derry et al., 2019) – pregabalin effective in post-herpetic neuralgia and diabetic neuropathy (NNT ~5–8 at 300–600 mg).
Dizziness, drowsiness and weight gain may occur
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
